rows.difference: Lean accepts #xG and #xg, which the passages exclude; it rejects #x9, which they allow.
Lean accepts :0 and :assert, although the passages require a simple-symbol suffix, excluding a digit at the start and reserved words. It also rejects :a9, which the passages allow.
Lean rejects the character 9 (decimal code 57), which both passages allow as a digit.

Lean accepts a final semicolon-only comment, or ;abc at end of input without a line break. The passages require a subsequent line-breaking character to end a comment. Conversely, commentAtEnd itself rejects ;abc followed by LF as a whole match, although that is a complete comment in the passages.
Lean rejects tab (decimal code 9) as whitespace; both passages allow it.
In version 2.7, Lean accepts an application with no arguments, serialized as (f). The passage requires at least one argument and therefore excludes (f).
Lean rejects a string literal containing an actual tab, such as the byte sequence [34, 9, 34]. The passages allow whitespace characters, including tab, inside string literals.
Lean accepts 00.1, which the passages exclude because its integer part is not a numeral. Lean rejects 9.0 and 0.9, both allowed by the passages.
Lean rejects a9 as a simple symbol in both versions 2.5 and 2.7, although the passages allow it.
Lean accepts 00 and 0012 as numerals, which the passages exclude; it rejects 9 and 19, which the passages allow.
Lean rejects a quoted symbol containing an actual tab, such as the byte sequence [124, 9, 124]. The passages allow it.

For version 2.5, Lean rejects (declare-const x Int), although 2.5-p090-04 explicitly permits it. Also, via Term.Valid, Lean accepts (assert (f)) in both 2.0 and 2.5, even though (f) has no argument and is not a term under the referenced grammar.

Read literally as supplied, the cited production excludes uppercase B through Z, while Lean accepts them; for example Lean accepts B as a letter. This judgment does not silently correct the printed uppercase endpoint A to Z.

At version 2.5, Lean rejects let (and assert) as a simple symbol, although the cited 2.5 appendix production allows these nonempty, letter-only sequences. At version 2.7, the reserved-word exclusion agrees with the cited prose.
Lean accepts #b2 (and #b102) as a binary literal; both cited passages exclude the digit 2.
At version 2.5, Lean rejects (echo ""), which the cited 2.5 command production allows.

Lean rejects the valid four-double-quote token (character codes [34,34,34,34]), which denotes a string containing one double quote. It instead accepts the token with codes [34,92,34,34] (opening quote, backslash, quote, closing quote), which is not a complete valid literal under the passages' doubled-quote rule.

Lean accepts :1 as a keyword, while the passages require a simple-symbol suffix, which cannot start with a digit. It also accepts :let, whose suffix is a reserved word and therefore is not a simple symbol in version 2.7.
At version 2.7, Lean accepts (let () 0), while the cited term production requires at least one variable binding.
Lean accepts a quoted symbol containing a backslash, for example the five-character token |a\b| (codes [124,97,92,98,124]); the passages forbid backslash inside quoted symbols.

Lean accepts ;abc at end of input, with no following line feed or carriage return, as a comment. The cited definition requires the comment to end with a subsequent line-breaking character and supplies no end-of-file exception.
Lean rejects 1.1 and 0.0 as decimals, although both passages allow them: choose zero occurrences of the optional fractional-prefix zero, then the numeral 1 or 0 respectively.
